exam: What is the first investigation you would order for a patient with a unilateral vesicular rash on the thoracic region? — Clinical diagnosis; if atypical, obtain Tzanck smear or PCR to confirm VZV.
A 68‑year‑old presents with V1 dermatomal pain and a few vesicles on the forehead. What urgent step is required? — Immediate ophthalmology referral to assess for keratitis or uveitis.
How does immunosuppression alter the management of herpes zoster? — Start antiviral within 72 h, consider intravenous therapy, add prophylactic antibiotics if bacterial superinfection risk is high.
Explain why post‑herpetic neuralgia is more common in older patients. — Age‑related decline in nerve regeneration and immune response leads to prolonged neuropathic pain.
You have no PCR facility. How do you proceed with treatment? — Treat empirically based on classic dermatomal pain and vesicles; monitor for complications.

Differentiate herpes zoster from herpes simplex infection on the basis of clinical features. — Zoster follows a single dermatome, has a prodrome of pain, and occurs in older or immunocompromised patients; HSV is usually localized to mucocutaneous sites and recurs at the same site.
Why are systemic steroids generally avoided in herpes zoster? — They suppress cell‑mediated immunity, potentially worsening viral replication and increasing complication risk.

What vaccination strategy would you recommend for a 55‑year‑old HIV‑positive patient in a low‑resource setting? — Offer the recombinant zoster vaccine if available; otherwise, emphasize early antiviral treatment and education.
ai.title: Herpes Zoster (Shingles)
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Reactivation of latent varicella‑zoster virus causes a painful, dermatomal vesicular rash. Diagnosis is clinical, but severity, immunosuppression and complications guide management.

b: Clinical diagnosis: unilateral, dermatomal vesicles with burning pain
Typical latency period: years to decades
Confirmatory test (if atypical): Tzanck smear, PCR of vesicle fluid
sections.p: Herpes zoster is the reactivation of varicella‑zoster virus (VZV) that has remained dormant in dorsal root or cranial nerve ganglia after primary chicken‑pox infection.

b: Mild: <2 dermatomes, no ocular or systemic involvement
Moderate: 2–3 dermatomes, severe pain, possible secondary bacterial infection
Severe: >3 dermatomes, ophthalmic zoster, disseminated vesicles, immunocompromise
sections.p: Severity is graded by extent of skin involvement, pain intensity and presence of complications such as ophthalmic involvement or disseminated disease.

b: Age >60 years
HIV infection
Chronic steroid use or other immunosuppressants
Malnutrition, severe malaria, TB co‑infection
sections.p: Reactivation is triggered by waning cell‑mediated immunity, especially in older adults or those with immunosuppressive conditions common in low‑resource settings.

b: Pain may be severe and precede visible lesions
Vesicles evolve to pustules then crust over in 7–10 days
Post‑herpetic neuralgia (PHN) risk increases with age
sections.p: Prodrome of burning, itching or stabbing pain precedes the rash by 1–5 days. The rash appears as grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, respecting a single dermatome.
If PCR or Tzanck smear is unavailable, treat clinically based on typical dermatomal rash and pain.

t.a: Tzanck smear / PCR of vesicle fluid
t.b: Confirms VZV when rash is atypical or in immunocompromised patients — presence of multinucleated giant cells or VZV DNA confirms diagnosis
Detects leukocytosis suggesting secondary bacterial infection — neutrophil rise prompts antibiotics
Identifies underlying immunosuppression that raises risk of severe disease — positive result changes management to include prophylaxis
Detects keratitis or uveitis — urgent referral to ophthalmology required

b: Ophthalmic (V1) zoster → keratitis, vision loss
Disseminated zoster → >20 lesions outside primary dermatome, organ involvement
Post‑herpetic neuralgia → chronic pain >3 months
Bacterial superinfection → cellulitis, sepsis
sections.p: Complications can be sight‑threatening, neurologic or systemic, especially in immunocompromised patients.

b: Antiviral (e.g., oral aciclovir, valaciclovir, famciclovir) started within 72 h of rash onset – inhibits VZV replication
Analgesia: NSAIDs first line, add gabapentin or tricyclic antidepressant for neuropathic pain
Topical care: clean lesions, apply sterile dressings, consider antiseptic if bacterial infection suspected
Avoid systemic steroids unless severe ophthalmic involvement and under specialist guidance
sections.p: Treat early to reduce pain, hasten rash healing and lower PHN risk. Combine antiviral therapy with analgesia and, when needed, antibiotics.

b: Review at 2 weeks for healing and secondary infection
Assess for PHN; refer to pain clinic if persistent
Vaccinate eligible adults ≥50 y or immunocompromised with recombinant zoster vaccine (if available)
Educate on early presentation for future recurrences
sections.p: Monitor pain resolution, wound healing and signs of complications. Vaccination reduces future episodes.

b: Contact dermatitis – usually bilateral, no vesicle grouping
Herpes simplex – clusters on lips or genitals, not dermatomal
Dermatitis herpetiformis – grouped vesicles on extensor surfaces, associated with celiac disease
sections.p: Other painful dermatomal eruptions can mimic shingles.

b: Normal CBC does not exclude bacterial superinfection; watch clinical signs
Negative Tzanck smear in early lesions – repeat or treat empirically
sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely reassuring.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid visual loss or eye pain (possible ocular involvement)
Fever >38 °C with spreading vesicles beyond one dermatome
Severe, unrelenting pain unresponsive to analgesics
Signs of sepsis: tachycardia, hypotension, altered mental status
